extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of art history/architecture, architects, and scholars of Venetian Gothic art
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and analysis of the form, iconography, and design principles of Venetian Gothic architecture, with attention to the Ducal Palace's façades, doorways, sculptural programs (months), and interior arrangements. Useful for architectural historians, conservators, and designers seeking period-accurate features and evaluative principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: June — Reaping
rubrics_metrics.description: 6. JUNE. Reaping. The corn and sickle sculptured with singular care and precision, in bold relief, and the zodiacal sign, the Crab, above, also worked with great spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Month-figure should show clear agricultural implement (corn and sickle) and zodiac sign; execution in bold relief and carefully wrought detail, especially flora among long grass. Variants in manuscripts may show alternate labors (e.g., sheep-shearing) or accessory objects (fagot or barrel).

rubrics_metrics.name: July — Mowing
rubrics_metrics.description: 7. JULY. Mowing. A very interesting piece of sculpture, owing to the care with which the flowers are wrought out among the long grass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: July is conventionally shown mowing (sometimes reaping); emphasis placed on articulation of flowers and grass; sculptural interest lies in delicate vegetal carving.

rubrics_metrics.name: August — Sleeping/Asleep with Virgin above
rubrics_metrics.description: 8. AUGUST. Peculiarly represented in this archivolt, sitting in a chair, with his head upon his hand, as if asleep; the Virgin (the zodiacal sign) above him, lifting up her hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Northern variants instead depict threshing or grape-gathering; Italian/peculiar versions may show repose with associated zodiacal figure. Choice of depiction should reflect local climate/agricultural practice or iconographic program.

rubrics_metrics.name: September — Bearing home grapes / Portioning harvest
rubrics_metrics.description: 9. SEPTEMBER. Bearing home grapes in a basket. Almost always sowing, in Northern work. By Spenser ... employed in gathering in the general harvest, and portioning it out with the Scales, his zodiacal sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: September's representation varies regionally (grape-bearing vs sowing); may incorporate zodiacal symbol (Scales) and narrative act (portioning). Accuracy to local tradition is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: October — Digging / Vintager/Sowing variants
rubrics_metrics.description: 10. OCTOBER. Wearing a conical hat, and digging busily with a long spade. In Northern work he is sometimes a vintager, sometimes beating the acorns out of an oak to feed swine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: October commonly shows digging; alternate local labors (vintaging, beating oak) are acceptable depending on regional agricultural systems; costume (conical hat) and tool depiction are important details.

rubrics_metrics.name: November — Catching birds / Killing pigs variants
rubrics_metrics.description: 11. NOVEMBER. Seems to be catching small birds in a net. He is nearly always killing pigs; sometimes beating the oak for them; with Spenser, fatting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: November often associated with pig-killing or related autumnal tasks; occasional unusual depictions (bird-catching) should be noted as rare variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: December — Killing swine / Baking variants
rubrics_metrics.description: 12. DECEMBER. Killing swine. It is hardly ever that this employment is not given to one or other of the terminal months of the year. If not so engaged, December is usually putting new loaves into the oven; sometimes killing oxen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal-month activities typically involve slaughtering or feasting; alternate bakery or ox-killing scenes are acceptable; iconography should reflect seasonal domestic economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional labors-of-the-month program (regional variations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallel tables show how the labors of each month vary among St. Mark's archivolt and several Northern and French, English, Flemish manuscripts and carvings, indicating that the month's employment expresses varieties of climate and agricultural system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or producing month-cycle sculpture, account for regional climate, agricultural calendar, and manuscript tradition; expect and document systematic variation (e.g., when September is vintaging, October is sowing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doorway archology: absence of 'fantastic fourth order' in doorways
rubrics_metrics.description: No arches of the fantastic fourth order occur in any doorways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating or reconstructing Venetian doorways, do not employ the most fantastical/ornamental (fourth-order) arch forms — they are absent from historic doorways; use authentic orders compatible with period examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doorways: early and frequent use of pure pointed arch
rubrics_metrics.description: The pure pointed arch occurs earlier, and much oftener, in doorways than in window-heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pointed arches are characteristic of doorways in Venetian Gothic and should be favored in period-accurate work for entrances rather than necessarily at windowheads in early examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early small entrances often square-headed
rubrics_metrics.description: The entrance itself, if small, is nearly always square-headed in the earliest examples, without any arch above, but afterwards the arch is thrown across above the lintel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small-door restorations or studies should check for square-headed early forms; later modifications introduce an arch above the lintel — record sequencing when dating or restoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tympanum treatment over lintel
rubrics_metrics.description: The interval between the two, or tympanum, is filled with sculpture, or closed by iron bars, with sometimes a projecting gable, to form a porch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tympana should commonly contain sculptural subject matter (family shield, religious imagery) or functional closures (iron bars); porches may have projecting gables — these are standard treatments to consider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Door-head subjects: family shield protected by an angel
rubrics_metrics.description: The door-head is charged either with delicate ornaments and inlaid patterns in variously colored brick, or with sculptures, consisting always of the shield or crest of the family, protected by an angel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculptural programs above entrances typically center on heraldry (shield/crest) and an angelic protector; alternate human figures or grotesques may be used but an angel is often introduced above the shield in full examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venetian doorway theory: family-name + divine defence + benediction
rubrics_metrics.description: In the earlier ages ... the name of the family is told, and together with it there is always an intimation that they have placed their defence and their prosperity in God's hands; frequently accompanied with some general expression of benediction to the person passing over the threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inscriptions and sculptural program over doors should communicate family identity and a pious invocation/blessing; this was the guiding 'theory' of early Venetian doorways and is a key interpretive element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplified heraldic representation where sculpture is inadmissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Where elaborate sculpture of this kind is inadmissible, the shield is merely represented as suspended by a leather thong; and a cross is introduced above the archivolt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low-budget or constrained executions substitute painted or carved-simplified heraldry (suspended shield, cross) for full sculptural groups; assess material/space constraints when judging authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venetian heraldry preference: angels rather than beasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Venetian heraldry requires no beasts for supporters, but usually prefers angels, neither the supporters nor crests forming any necessary part of Venetian bearings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations or restorations of Venetian coats-of-arms should favor angelic supporters and avoid continental beast-supporters unless contextual evidence indicates otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renaissance substitution of classical ornament for religious emblems
rubrics_metrics.description: The Renaissance architects perceived the irrationality of all this, cut away both crosses and angels, and substituted heads of satyrs, which were the proper presiding deities of Venice in the Renaissance periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dating decorative changes: replacement of crosses/angels with satyr-heads and classical motifs indicates Renaissance-era alterations; presence of such elements signals later intervention and informs conservation decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of religious inscriptions into Renaissance
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of employing some religious symbol, or writing some religious legend, over the door of the house, does not entirely disappear until far into the period of the Renaissance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect religious inscriptions/legends on doorways well into Renaissance times; loss of such inscriptions may indicate later Protestant or modern modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gateway → long interior court plan with external grand staircase
rubrics_metrics.description: The gateways ... almost universally lead, in the earlier palaces, into a long interior court, round which the mass of the palace is built; and in which its first story is reached by a superb external staircase, sustained on four or five pointed arches gradually increasing as they ascend, both in height and span,—this change in their size being ... peculiar to Venice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing Venetian palace plans, look for the long central court and external staircase feature; the stair's pointed arches that increase in size are a regional/period diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wells as sculptural capitals with foliage and family shield
rubrics_metrics.description: The Gothic wells ... are little varied; they being, in almost every case, treated like colossal capitals of pillars, with foliage at the angles, and the shield of the family upon their sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-heads should be read as important sculptural elements; expect foliated carving and heraldry. Byzantine wells (octagonal, font-like) are rarer survivals and should be noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement of interior apartments: noble hall and subsidiary rooms
rubrics_metrics.description: The interior apartments always consist of one noble hall on the first story, often on the second also, extending across the entire depth of the house, and lighted in front by the principal groups of its windows, while smaller apartments open from it on either side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess interior plans for a primary ceremonial hall occupying breadth of building with subsidiary side rooms; window placement is coordinated to light these halls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceiling treatment: bold horizontal carved and gilded beams (later often painted)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ceilings, where they remain untouched, are of bold horizontal beams, richly carved and gilded; but few of these are left from the true Gothic times, the Venetian interiors having, in almost every case, been remodelled by the Renaissance architects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original Gothic interiors favor exposed, ornamented beam-ceilings; later renovations commonly covered or repainted them with major decorative schemes (Veronese, Titian, Tintoret). Identify layering when dating or conserving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Façade composition: smooth wall sustained on two tiers of pillars
rubrics_metrics.description: It will be observed that the façade is composed of a smooth mass of wall, sustained on two tiers of pillars, one above the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Façade analysis should note the two-tiered arcade/pillar support system as a defining structural and visual device in the Ducal Palace; use section studies to confirm load-bearing organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basilica-like structural logic for façades and interior stories
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inner floors and walls of the stories A, B were removed, there could be left merely the form of a basilica,—two high walls, carried on ranges of shafts, and roofed by a low gable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret multi-story palace façades as adaptations of basilica form; this informs how to read vertical organization and how later insertions (floors/partitions) altered an originally single-volume logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritizing interior function and decoration over external symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the most remarkable instances ... of the daring sacrifice of symmetry to convenience ... The old Venetian thought of the honor of the paintings, and the comfort of the senate, before his own reputation. He unhesitatingly raised the large windows to their proper position with reference to the interior of the chamber, and suffered the external appearance to take care of itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging Venetian Gothic façades, accept asymmetry or variation in window placement as intentional, driven by interior lighting and pictorial programs; such sacrifices of exterior symmetry to interior exigency are to be read positively rather than as faults.
